overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of what pretraining a large language model takes and what it leaves behind. You'll be asked about pretraining data, compute and training runs, scale and the bitter lesson, and what a trained model retains.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: A language model answers detailed questions about widely discussed topics in English and does poorly on questions about a language with few speakers online. What best explains the difference?

options.html: The model's developer blocked questions in other languages
options.text: The model's developer blocked questions in other languages
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nothing suggests a block. A model's knowledge follows its pretraining corpus, and a corpus built mostly from the web has far more English text than text in languages with a small web presence.

options.html: The model's tokens can represent only English words
options.text: The model's tokens can represent only English words
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Tokens can represent text in any language. The difference comes from the corpus, which has far more English text than text in languages with a small web presence.

options.html: The model's corpus held far more English text
options.text: The model's corpus held far more English text
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A model's strengths follow the proportions of its pretraining corpus. Web-based corpora over-represent English and under-represent languages whose speakers publish little online.

options.html: The model's context window is shorter for other languages
options.text: The model's context window is shorter for other languages
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The context window limits how much text a model takes in, whatever the language. The difference comes from the corpus, which has far more English text.

forms.stemHtml: Which statement correctly distinguishes training from inference?

options.html: Training adjusts the parameters, and inference leaves them fixed
options.text: Training adjusts the parameters, and inference leaves them fixed
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Training happens once per model and changes its parameters. Inference is the running of the finished model, and it happens every time the model is used without changing anything.

options.html: Training happens with every message, and inference happens only once
options.text: Training happens with every message, and inference happens only once
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. It's the other way around. Training happens once per model and adjusts the parameters, and inference happens with every use and leaves them fixed.

options.html: Training needs no specialized chips, and inference needs thousands
options.text: Training needs no specialized chips, and inference needs thousands
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Training is the stage that needs many thousands of chips for months. Training adjusts the parameters, and inference leaves them fixed.

options.html: Training uses the model's replies, and inference uses the web crawl
options.text: Training uses the model's replies, and inference uses the web crawl
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Training uses the text corpus. Training adjusts the parameters, and inference is the running of the finished model with its parameters fixed.

forms.stemHtml: What is the central claim of Rich Sutton's essay "The Bitter Lesson"?

options.html: Building in human knowledge is what makes AI systems succeed
options.text: Building in human knowledge is what makes AI systems succeed
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Sutton argues the opposite. His claim is that general methods which make use of more computation have, over time, beaten approaches built on human knowledge of a task.

options.html: AI research has made little real progress in seventy years
options.text: AI research has made little real progress in seventy years
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Sutton describes large advances. His claim is that general methods which make use of more computation have beaten approaches built on human knowledge of a task.

options.html: Larger models are too expensive to be worth training
options.text: Larger models are too expensive to be worth training
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Sutton doesn't argue against cost. His claim is that general methods which make use of more computation have beaten approaches built on human knowledge of a task.

options.html: General methods that use more computation win over time
options.text: General methods that use more computation win over time
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Sutton argues from cases such as chess, Go, and speech recognition that search and learning, given more computation, outperformed systems built around researchers' own understanding of the task.

forms.stemHtml: A chatbot with no search tool is asked about an event that took place after its knowledge cutoff. What should you expect?

options.html: An accurate answer, since the model keeps learning from the web
options.text: An accurate answer, since the model keeps learning from the web
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The parameters are frozen when training ends. The model has nothing about the event, so it may say it doesn't know or may produce a plausible but unsupported answer.

options.html: No real information, though the reply may still sound confident
options.text: No real information, though the reply may still sound confident
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Nothing after the cutoff is reflected in the parameters. The model may say it doesn't know, or it may produce a fluent answer from older patterns.

options.html: An accurate answer, since the event is stored in the context window
options.text: An accurate answer, since the event is stored in the context window
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The context window holds only the text in front of the model, and nothing here put the event there. The model has no real information about it, though its reply may still sound confident.

options.html: An error message, since the model checks dates before it replies
options.text: An error message, since the model checks dates before it replies
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model has no step that checks dates. It has no real information about the event, and it may still produce a confident-sounding reply.

forms.stemHtml: Researchers prompted an earlier language model many times and found passages in its output that matched its training text word for word. Which conclusions does the study support? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: A model can retain some training passages exactly
options.text: A model can retain some training passages exactly
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The study recovered several hundred word-for-word passages, which shows that some memorization occurs.

options.html: A model keeps a full copy of all its training text
options.text: A model keeps a full copy of all its training text
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The extracted passages were a tiny fraction of the training text. Most text is retained only as patterns.

options.html: Text that appeared in one document can be memorized
options.text: Text that appeared in one document can be memorized
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The authors report that their method worked on some passages found in just one document in the training data.

options.html: A model looks up its training text when it replies
options.text: A model looks up its training text when it replies
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model doesn't consult its training text. The passages were reproduced from the parameters.

options.html: "It stores nothing" is too strong a claim
options.text: "It stores nothing" is too strong a claim
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Most text is compressed into patterns, and some passages still survive word for word.

title: Pretraining at scale: data, compute, and cost
